slides.title: Key questions

paragraphs.text: Key questions
Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027, using only its $12.0M of cash and keeping 12 months of runway?
Is the market growing, and has any operator shown it can make money in it?
Can an order make money after paying for the rider and the dark store?
Do customers order often enough to repay what it costs to win them?
Does the plan keep 12 months of runway, and is it the best use of the cash?
What should the board decide in January 2027, and what would reopen the question?
Decision maker
Success criteria
Timing
Out of scope
Board of Parcelbird (two founders, two investors), deciding whether to fund the launch

A path to profitability within the current $12.0M of cash, with no new round; At least 12 months of runway at all times; Orders that make money after site costs on inputs already observed, not only in the plan
Board meeting, January 2027
A new funding round; Other cities; Non-grocery delivery

slides.title: Executive summary

paragraphs.text: Executive summary
Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; put the cash into the software business, which can break even without new funding
The market grows about 40% a year, but no operator has yet shown it can make money in it
–	Zipcart loses $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 on each order
At benchmark inputs an order loses about $6.2 after site costs; the plan needs every driver above the best site
–	Break-even would need a $63 basket, against the $34 median
Few customers keep ordering, so the $38 it costs to win each one is slow or impossible to recover
–	Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three
The launch leaves about 6 months of runway even if all goes to plan; the software can break even on current cash
–	The software breaks even in early 2029 with about $5.4M left
Decline the launch; put $0.8M a year into the software and store-based delivery for grocers, with gates to reopen
–	Reopen only when a customer site makes money after site costs
